newsitem.title: USA: Florida barred from future damages in smoking case.
newsitem.headline: Florida barred from future damages in smoking case.

text.p: Tobacco companies won a big victory Thursday in Florida's lawsuit to recoup the costs of treating smokers when a judge barred the state from seeking $16 billion in anticipated future damages.

"The tobacco industry is correct in that the law does not allow for collecting now future damages," Circuit Judge Harold Cohen said in issuing the ruling, the first to address the issue of such damages in a state lawsuit against the industry.

But the judge also handed the industry a defeat. In a separate ruling, he upheld a state law on documents in lawsuits that could lead to the publication of thousands of pages of tobacco company documents.

Cohen, who ruled that Florida's Sunshine in Litigation Act was constitutional, directed a special master to review the documents to see if trade secrets in them contain evidence of a public hazard. The state law says documents with trade secrets can be made public if they involve such a hazard.

Florida is one of 40 states that have sued cigarette makers over the public health costs of treating sick smokers. The volume of lawsuits was a major impetus behind the sweeping settlement agreement announced last week in which cigarette makers agreed to pay $368.5 billion over 25 years.
Florida is going ahead with its lawsuit in spite of the agreement, which still must be approved by Congress.

Cohen's ruling to eliminate future damages still allows Florida to seek $1 billion in actual damages, which could be tripled if the state can prove the tobacco companies engaged in criminal conduct in the sale and marketing of cigarettes.
Cohen also encouraged the state to appeal his ruling.

Because of "the great public importance of this issue -- and in light of the trial -- I encourage the state to make a quick appeal of this ruling so that, if I am reversed, future damages can be included in the case and we can proceed from there," the judge said.

The ruling came in a pretrial review as the judge sought to narrow what may be presented to the jury during the Medicaid trial, which is set to start Aug. 4. Mississippi's case against cigarette makers is set to be the first state Medicaid case to go trial, on July 7, but sources in the tobacco settlement believe that case may not go forward.
Since Monday, tobacco company attorneys have been hammering away at Florida's case, eliminating many of the weapons the state had hoped to use against them.
The judge said he understood the problem that eliminating future damages would force the state's attorneys to return to court again and again to seek future payments.
"If the legislature had intended future damages to be included in the statute, it should have clearly said so. It didn't, and I am comfortable with (this) ruling," Cohen said.
The judge was referring to Florida's 1994 Third Party Liability Act, which allowed the state to bring the Medicaid lawsuit against tobacco companies.
Tobacco attorneys smiled when Cohen announced his ruling on damages.
"We are delighted with the ruling," Murray Garnick, an attorney for Philip Morris Cos. Inc., said in an interview. "We think the judge properly and correctly read the statute."
Robert Montgomery, one of Florida's attorneys, said he was intimately aware of the problems that Cohen was grappling with in reaching his decision.
But, he said, "Our position is that the entire situation should be resolved now so that we should not have to return to the court again and again to seek reimbursement."
